messages.content: A red oil-can light just came on while I was driving on the highway. The car sounds fine. Can I make it to the next exit, about six miles?

That light is a stop-now light, not a finish-your-trip light. It means oil PRESSURE has dropped below the safe minimum — the bearings inside the engine are being starved of the oil film they ride on. An engine can sound perfectly normal while this is happening and still be destroyed within a minute or two of running; the damage is silent until it suddenly isn't.

Pull onto the shoulder as soon as it's safe, switch the engine off, and leave it off. Do not restart it 'just to check.' Call for a tow.

Once you're stopped, there is one owner-level check worth doing while you wait: pull the dipstick (your manual shows where). If the oil level is far below the marks, that may explain the pressure loss — but even then, the engine does not get restarted. Low pressure has several causes (low level, a failing pump, internal wear), and only a shop can sort out which one you have and whether damage was already done. Six miles at highway speed on no oil pressure is very likely the difference between a repair and a replacement engine.
My oil light flickers at red lights when the engine is hot, then goes out as soon as I accelerate. What's going on?

That pattern is a classic low-oil-pressure-at-idle symptom, and it's worth taking seriously even though the light behaves itself at speed. Oil pressure is lowest at idle: the pump turns slowest there, and hot oil is thinner, so a marginal system shows its weakness at a stoplight first. As revs rise, the pump spins faster and pressure recovers enough to switch the light off.

Your one owner-level check: with the engine off and cool, check the dipstick. If the level is low, topping up to the full mark with the oil grade in your manual may cure it — a low level means less oil for the pump to pick up, and sloshing at idle makes it worse.

If the level is already correct, the causes move inside the engine: worn bearings letting pressure leak away, a tired pump, a clogged pickup screen. Those are shop diagnoses, and this is not a 'watch it for a few months' symptom — pressure that's marginal today tends to get worse, and the end of that road is the solid red light from the previous scenario. Book it in soon and mention the exact pattern: flickers hot, at idle only. That detail saves diagnostic time.
I checked my oil and it's a quart low, but no warning light has ever come on. Is the light broken?

Probably not — the light and the dipstick are measuring two different things, and this is one of the most useful distinctions an owner can learn. The dipstick measures oil LEVEL: how much oil is in the sump. The dashboard light (on most cars) measures oil PRESSURE: whether the pump is delivering oil to the bearings at adequate pressure right now.

An engine a quart low usually still makes full pressure — the pump's pickup sits low in the sump and stays submerged. So no light is normal. The light is a last-resort alarm for pressure collapse, not a low-level reminder; by the time it comes on while driving, you're often already in trouble. That's exactly why the manual schedules dipstick checks instead of trusting the light.

What to do: top up to the full mark with the exact grade your manual specifies, then figure out where the quart went. Check again in 500 miles. If it's another quart down, the engine is burning or leaking oil at roughly a quart per 500 miles, and that rate — measured, not guessed — is what to tell a mechanic. (A few newer cars do have a true low-level warning; your manual's symbol pages will say whether yours is one.)
My check engine light came on yesterday. It's on steady, and the car drives completely normally. How urgent is this?

A steady check engine light with a car that runs normally is a 'soon, not now' problem: something in the emissions or engine-management system has reported a fault, the car is protecting itself fine, and you should book a diagnostic appointment in the coming days rather than ignore it for months.

Before you pay for anything, do the one free owner check: the fuel cap. A loose or poorly sealed cap is one of the most common causes of this light, because the system pressure-tests the fuel tank's vapor lines and a loose cap fails the test. Unscrew it, reseat it until it clicks, and drive normally for a few days — if the cap was the cause, the light typically clears itself after several trips.

If it stays on, a shop will read the stored code. Understand what that gets you: a code names a system or a reading that's out of range — it is the start of a diagnosis, not the diagnosis itself.

Two changes would upgrade the urgency immediately: the light starts FLASHING, or the car develops symptoms — rough running, stalling, loss of power, strange smells. Either one moves it from 'book it this week' to 'deal with it today.'
The check engine light in my car started flashing and the engine feels rough and shaky. I have a 20-minute drive home. What should I do?

Do not drive it home like that. A flashing check engine light means something specific and different from a steady one: the engine is misfiring — one or more cylinders aren't firing properly — and unburned fuel is being dumped into the exhaust, where it can overheat and destroy the catalytic converter in minutes. The shaking you feel is the misfire itself.

The converter is an expensive part, and the misfire can also signal something worse developing. So: slow down, avoid hills and heavy throttle if you must move the car a short distance to a safe place, and get it towed or drive it gently the shortest possible distance to a shop — not twenty minutes home and then to a shop tomorrow.

Common causes a shop will check include a failed ignition coil, a dead spark plug, or a fuel injector problem — often a single cylinder, and frequently a straightforward repair if the converter hasn't been cooked. The flashing light is the car telling you the difference between 'fault recorded' and 'damage in progress.' Believe it.
How do I know whether a warning light means 'tow it' or 'drive it to the shop'? I can never tell.

Use three questions, in this order.

1. What color is it? Red means stop — oil pressure, coolant temperature, brake system, charging on some cars. Amber or yellow means caution: get it looked at soon, and drive gently in the meantime. Green and blue are information, not warnings at all — high beams, turn signals, cruise control.

2. Is it flashing? A flashing check engine light is the big exception to 'amber means soon' — flashing means a misfire is actively damaging the catalytic converter, so that one is stop-and-tow behavior in an amber light.

3. What does the car feel like? Symptoms outrank symbols. A brake pedal that sinks, steering that's suddenly heavy, steam from under the hood, a temperature gauge pinned at the top, or a loss of power — any of these mean stop now regardless of what the lights say. Conversely, a steady amber light with a car that drives, steers, and brakes completely normally is generally a careful drive to a scheduled appointment.

Your owner's manual has a page or two with every symbol your car can show and what the maker says to do about each. Read it once, on a calm afternoon, not on the shoulder of a highway.
The tire-pressure light came on this morning. It was the first really cold night of the year. The tires look fine. Is it a false alarm?

It's probably a true alarm about a small thing. Tire pressure falls as temperature falls — roughly 1 psi for every 10°F (about 0.07 bar per 5-6°C) the air inside cools. A tire that was borderline in September can easily be 3-4 psi low after the first cold snap, and the TPMS light is set to come on when a tire is about 25% below its specified pressure.

'They look fine' doesn't settle it — a tire 25% low often looks normal, because the sidewall is stiff. Get a gauge on all four (a simple stick or dial gauge costs very little) and compare against the pressure on the driver's door-jamb sticker — not the 'max press' molded into the tire sidewall, which is a ceiling, not a target. Inflate to the sticker number, ideally first thing in the morning when the tires are cold.

If one tire is much lower than the other three, that's not weather — that's a leak, and it needs a shop. And if all four were low, make a note: pressure gets checked monthly from now on, because it drifts down slowly even without a puncture.
My tire pressure light blinks for about a minute every time I start the car, then stays on solid. The pressures are all correct — I checked. What's it telling me?

That blink-then-solid pattern is the system reporting on itself, and it means something different from the plain low-pressure warning. When the light flashes at startup and then goes solid, the TPMS is saying: 'I have a fault in my own system' — most often a sensor inside one of the wheels whose battery has died. Those batteries typically last 5-10 years and aren't replaceable separately from the sensor.

Because you verified the pressures with a gauge and they're correct, the tires are fine to drive on — you've done the important part, which is confirming the actual air. What you've lost is the watchdog: with the system faulted, it may not warn you about a genuine low tire, so your monthly gauge checks now carry the whole job.

A tire shop can identify which sensor has gone quiet with a scan tool and replace it; it usually makes sense to have this done at your next tire service rather than as an emergency visit. One caution: if the light ever comes on solid WITHOUT the startup blink and stays on, treat it as a pressure warning again and check the tires — same lamp, two different messages, and the blink at startup is how you tell them apart.
A red battery-shaped light came on while I was driving. Everything still works. How long have I got?

That light means the alternator has stopped charging the battery — the car's entire electrical system is now running off the battery alone, and the battery is a bucket with a hole in it. Depending on the car and the battery's condition, you typically have somewhere in the range of 15-30 minutes of driving before the voltage drops enough to stall the engine — treat it as 'get somewhere now,' not as a number to spend.

Use those minutes deliberately. Turn off every electrical load you don't need: air conditioning, heated seats, rear defroster, blower fan, even the radio. Headlights are the trade-off — keep them if visibility or law requires them, they're a real draw but safety comes first. Drive directly to the nearest repair shop or safe place. Do NOT turn the engine off on the way 'to save the battery' — restarting is the single biggest electrical load there is, and a car that was running may not restart.

Once parked, expect the car to need a tow or a jump-and-charge diagnosis. The shop will test the alternator and the battery; note that a battery run flat like this may itself be damaged, so 'just the alternator' sometimes becomes 'alternator, and the battery it took with it.'
Driving home, the battery light came on, the steering suddenly got very heavy, and then the temperature gauge started climbing. Three things at once?

One thing, most likely — and it's a stop-now situation. On many cars a single serpentine belt drives the alternator (charging), the power steering pump, and the water pump (coolant circulation). When that belt snaps or slips off, you lose all three at once: the battery light is the alternator quitting, the heavy steering is the pump quitting, and the climbing temperature is the coolant no longer circulating — the engine is still making full heat with no way to shed it.

Pull over and switch off as soon as you safely can. The steering will be heavy but the car remains steerable at low speed — it takes real effort, so choose your stopping spot early rather than fighting it through a curve. Do not be tempted to limp home: the temperature is the deadline, and an overheated engine can warp its cylinder head, turning a belt replacement into an engine-out repair.

This needs a tow. The good news is that the diagnosis is usually simple and the fix is a belt — unless the belt broke because one of the pulleys it drives has seized, which the shop will check by spinning each one by hand. Tell the tow driver and the shop the three symptoms together; that combination points straight at the belt.
My temperature gauge just went into the red and there's a wisp of steam from under the hood. I'm a mile from home. Surely a mile is OK?

A mile is not OK — this is one of the clearest stop lines in all of car ownership. The gauge in the red means the coolant is already boiling inside the engine, and the metal of the cylinder head is expanding unevenly. Driving on, even slowly, even a mile, is how a failed thermostat or a lost coolant hose turns into a warped head and a repair bill several times larger.

Pull over, switch the engine off, and let it sit. Two safety rules while you wait: do NOT open the hood and reach in immediately if steam is heavy, and NEVER open the radiator or coolant reservoir cap on a hot engine — the system is pressurized, and removing the cap releases a geyser of scalding coolant. Even the reservoir cap on many cars is a pressure cap. Hands off until the engine is fully cool, which takes the better part of an hour.

This car gets towed. When the shop finds the cause — a split hose, a stuck thermostat, a dead fan, a failed water pump — ask them to confirm the head gasket survived; catching that question early is much cheaper than discovering it later. The mile home is the most expensive mile you could drive.
A red light that says BRAKE came on in my dash. The parking brake is definitely off. The pedal feels... maybe a bit lower than usual? Can I drive it to the shop carefully?

No — with that light and a pedal that feels lower, this car should be towed, not driven carefully. The red BRAKE light has a few possible causes: the parking brake left on (you've ruled that out), brake fluid level low, or a fault in the hydraulic system. A pedal that rides lower than normal is exactly the symptom that separates 'low fluid because pads are worn' from 'fluid is escaping somewhere.'

Here is the one check you may do, parked, engine running: press the pedal firmly and hold it. A healthy pedal stays where it stops. A pedal that slowly sinks toward the floor under steady pressure means pressure is leaking away inside the system — and a system that leaks standing still will fail you at the worst moment moving. If it sinks, that's your answer: tow.

Even if the pedal feels firm, a red brake light is not a drive-and-see item. Brake work — lines, fluid, hydraulics — is professional territory, not an owner repair. The cost of a tow is small; the cost of discovering at 40 mph that the pedal was telling the truth is not one you pay in money.
The ABS light is on in my car but the brakes feel completely normal. Is it safe to drive?

Yes, with one clear understanding of what you've lost. The ABS light means the anti-lock system has found a fault in itself — a wheel-speed sensor is the most common culprit — and has switched itself off. Your regular hydraulic brakes are a separate system and they keep working normally, which is why the pedal feels fine.

What changes is behavior in a panic stop or on a slippery surface: without ABS, a hard brake application can lock the wheels, and a locked front wheel can't steer. So until it's fixed: leave more following distance, brake earlier and more gently in the wet, and if you ever do lock up in an emergency, ease off the pedal just enough to get the wheels rolling again — that's the job the ABS used to do for you.

Book the repair in the normal course of things — it's a 'this month' item, not a 'today' item, and it becomes more urgent if winter or rainy season is coming. One distinction to keep straight: ABS light alone, amber, normal pedal = drive carefully and schedule. The RED brake light, or any change in how the pedal feels, is a different and much more serious message — that combination means stop and tow.
The airbag light (it says SRS) stays on in my car. Everything else is fine. Can I just ignore it, and is it something I can fix myself?

Don't ignore it, and don't attempt it yourself — airbag systems are one of the true no-owner-work areas of a car. The light means the restraint system has detected a fault and has partly or fully disabled itself. The practical consequence: in a crash, one or more airbags may not deploy, and the seatbelt pretensioners may not fire. The car drives exactly the same, which is what makes this light easy to live with and dangerous to live with.

Why it's professional-only: airbags are pyrotechnic devices. Working around them without the proper disarming procedure risks deploying one into your face, and probing the wiring with ordinary test equipment can itself trigger a deployment or damage the control module. This is not caution-theater; it's the reason the manual will tell you nothing about servicing it.

Causes are often mundane — a sensor under a seat disturbed by something slid underneath, a connector, the clock-spring in the steering wheel — and diagnosis requires a scanner that can talk to the restraint module, which cheap code readers can't. Book it at a shop or dealer, mention whether anything changed recently (seat moved, something stored under it, a minor bump), and treat it as a genuine safety repair, not a cosmetic one.
I get confused by all the dashboard symbols. Is there a system to them, or do I just have to memorize forty icons?

There's a system, and it's mostly color. Learn the colors and you can triage any symbol you've never seen before.

Red = act now. Oil pressure, coolant temperature, brake system, and on some cars the charging system. Red means stop driving or stop soon — the car is telling you damage or danger is close.

Amber/yellow = soon. Check engine, ABS, TPMS, airbag, traction control. The car is drivable with care, and the repair belongs on this week's or this month's list, depending on the system. The one amber exception is a FLASHING check engine light, which behaves like a red.

Green and blue = information only. Turn signals, high beams (blue), cruise control, fog lights. These aren't warnings at all — they're the car confirming something is switched on.

After color, shape helps: a thermometer in wavy liquid is coolant temperature, an oil can is oil, a battery outline is charging, an exclamation mark in a horseshoe-ish bracket is tire pressure.

Then do the thing almost nobody does: spend ten minutes with the owner's manual's symbol pages once, in the driveway. The maker lists every lamp your specific car has, what it means, and what to do — that page is the authority, and it's much better learned calmly than at 70 mph.
My dash says 'MAINT REQD'. Is that the same as the check engine light? The car just had an oil change a few months ago.

Not the same thing at all, and the difference matters. 'Maintenance required' is a reminder counter, not a fault detector. The car simply counts miles (or days) since the reminder was last reset, and when the interval the maker chose runs out, it lights up to nudge you toward scheduled service. It has sensed nothing wrong.

The check engine light, by contrast, is the engine computer reporting that a monitored system produced a reading outside its limits — it always means a fault code has been stored.

Why yours is on a few months after an oil change: most likely the shop changed the oil but didn't reset the reminder, so the counter kept counting from the previous service. It happens constantly. Check your service sticker or invoice for the mileage of that oil change, compare it with the manual's oil interval, and if the oil is genuinely fresh, reset the reminder yourself — the procedure (a sequence with the trip button or a menu setting) is in the manual, and it's an owner task.

One discipline to keep: because the reminder is a dumb counter, never let anyone sell you work 'because the light is on.' The light says time has passed. Your service records say what was actually done.
When the low fuel light comes on, how much gas do I actually have left? My friend says she drives 40 miles on hers.

Your friend's number belongs to her car, not yours — the reserve varies a lot between models, and the honest answer lives in your owner's manual, which usually states the reserve amount directly ('the low fuel warning lights when approximately X gallons / liters remain').

As a rough orientation, most cars light the warning with about 10-15% of the tank left, often 1.5-3 gallons (6-11 liters). What that means in miles depends entirely on your fuel economy that day — the same 2 gallons are 70 highway miles or 35 miles of cold, short-trip city driving. The fuel gauge below a quarter tank is also at its least accurate; the float sits low in the tank and slopes and corners swing the reading.

Two habits worth having. First, treat the light as 'buy fuel at the next convenient station,' not as the start of a range challenge. Second, don't make running near-empty routine: in most cars the fuel pump sits inside the tank and is cooled by the fuel around it, and a habitually empty tank also concentrates any water and sediment at the pickup. Your friend's 40 miles is a story about her reserve and her commute; find your number in the manual and plan around it.
My EV flashed a little turtle symbol and the power dropped way down on the highway. It also mentioned the 12-volt battery last week. What happened, and can I check anything myself?

The turtle is your car's limp-home mode: it has detected a problem serious enough that it's limiting power to protect the battery and motors, while still letting you move. The correct response is the same as for any red-level warning — signal, move to the shoulder or the nearest safe exit at the reduced power you have, and stop. Don't try to 'push through' a turtle; power can step down further.

The 12-volt warning is a real clue, not a coincidence. EVs still carry an ordinary 12-volt battery, and it runs the computers, contactors, lights, and controls — the big traction battery can't even connect itself without 12-volt power. A dying 12-volt battery causes a remarkable share of EV 'won't start' and strange-warning events, and it's the one part of the car that behaves like a conventional car's battery.

What you may do: observe and report. Note the warnings in order, photograph the dash, and call for a tow or roadside service. What you may not do is anything involving the orange-cabled high-voltage system — no opening, probing, or jump procedures beyond what your manual explicitly describes for the 12-volt battery. Many EVs can have their 12-volt battery jump-started or replaced per the manual's procedure, but if the car has shown a turtle, let a professional make that call. Tell the shop about the 12-volt warning a week earlier — that timeline is diagnostic gold.
My brakes squeal when I'm braking gently, like coming up to a stop sign. If I brake harder it stops. Time for new brakes?

Very likely, yes — and that exact pattern is by design. Most brake pads have a small metal tab called a wear indicator. When the pad material wears down to near its limit, the tab starts touching the disc and produces a high-pitched squeal. It's deliberately most audible under light braking — gentle pressure lets the tab sing, while pressing harder changes the contact and can quiet it. The industry literally built a noise into the part to tell you this.

So treat the squeal as a scheduled message, not an emergency and not nothing: book a brake inspection in the next week or two. The shop will measure the remaining pad thickness in millimeters and check the discs. If the pads are at the wear limit, replacement now is pads-only money.

The reason not to stretch it: once the friction material is fully gone, the steel backing plate grinds directly on the disc. The sound changes from squeal to a harsh grinding, and from that point every stop is machining grooves into the disc — converting a pads job into a pads-and-discs job. Squeal = book it. Grind = book it today and drive gently and minimally until then.
There's a grinding noise every time I brake now, and the car feels like it takes longer to stop. I have a road trip this weekend. Can the brakes wait until Monday?

No — cancel the road trip plan for this car. Grinding under braking means the brake pads have worn through their friction material and steel is grinding on steel. Two things follow. First, stopping power is genuinely reduced, which matches what you're feeling — that longer stopping distance is not your imagination, and it gets worse as the surfaces chew each other up. Second, the damage compounds by the mile: the discs, which might have been reusable, are being grooved and scored right now, and in the worst case a disc can be ground thin enough to be unsafe.

This is a 'park it and book the earliest appointment' fault, not a 'drive carefully for a few more days' one. If the shop is close and the car still stops in a straight line with a firm pedal, a short, gentle, low-speed drive there is the maximum risk to accept — many people would tow it, and if the pedal feels soft or the car pulls, towing is the only answer.

For the future: grinding is almost always preceded by weeks of squealing from the wear indicators. That squeal is the cheap warning. When you hear this car start to squeal at stops again someday, that's the moment to book — it buys you the repair at the pads-only price.
My front-wheel-drive car clicks loudly when I turn into parking spaces. The tighter the turn, the faster the clicking. Straight driving is quiet. What is that?

That's the textbook signature of a worn outer CV (constant velocity) joint. Your front axles have joints at each end that let the wheels steer and move with the suspension while still being driven. The outer joint does the hardest work in a turn, and when its internal surfaces wear, it produces a clicking or snapping that repeats with wheel rotation — faster the tighter you turn, because the joint is working at its sharpest angle. Straight ahead, the joint is nearly unloaded and goes quiet, exactly as you describe.

Usually there's a backstory: the joint lives inside a rubber boot filled with grease, and the boot typically tore first — months ago — letting grease out and grit in. The joint has been wearing ever since.

This is a 'book it soon' repair, not a roadside one, but don't shelve it: a CV joint that clicks is announcing wear, and the end of that progression is a joint that fails and leaves the car unable to move. Mention which side clicks and in which direction of turn it clicks loudest — clicking on left turns generally indicts the right-side joint, because turning loads the outside wheel's joint hardest. That detail helps the shop confirm it on a lift in minutes.
There's a humming noise that gets louder and higher as I go faster. It doesn't change when I rev the engine at a stoplight, and it stays when I coast. Engine or something else?

You've already done the single most useful test in noise diagnosis, and it points away from the engine. The great separator is this: does the noise follow ROAD SPEED or ENGINE RPM? Revving at a standstill changed nothing and coasting changed nothing, so the noise is tied to how fast the wheels are turning — the suspects live downstream of the transmission: wheel bearings, tires, and (on some cars) the driveshaft.

A worn wheel bearing is the classic: a hum or growl that builds steadily with speed, often described as sounding like driving on a rumble strip or a distant propeller plane. One more observation you can safely make: on a gentle highway curve, does the hum get louder turning one way and quieter the other? Loading a bearing by turning toward it makes it louder; unloading it quiets it. That tells the shop which side to check first.

The other common cause is the tires themselves — uneven or cupped tread can hum convincingly like a bearing. A shop separates the two by lifting the car and spinning each wheel, and by inspecting the tread. Either way it's a 'book it this week' noise: a bearing that's audible is already worn, and left long enough it can develop play that affects the wheel itself.
My car has a droning hum that changes with engine revs — it does it in every gear, and even in Park when I rev the engine. Different problem from a wheel bearing?

Yes — and the Park test is what proves it. A wheel bearing can only make noise when the wheels turn. Your hum exists at a standstill with the engine revving, so it's locked to engine RPM, which puts the suspects on the engine itself or the accessories bolted to it and spun by its belt.

The usual list: a failing bearing in the alternator, an idler or tensioner pulley, the water pump, or the air-conditioning compressor — all of them spin whenever the engine runs, and all of them drone or whine in proportion to revs. An exhaust leak or a broken exhaust mount can also drone with RPM, though that usually has a harsher, buzzier character and changes with throttle load more than with revs alone.

What you can contribute as the owner is the pattern, recorded precisely: present in Park, follows revs, started when, getting worse how fast, any new warning lights (a battery light alongside would point at the alternator). Isolating WHICH pulley is a stethoscope job on a running engine — that's the shop's work, not something to do with your fingers near spinning belts.

Urgency: moderate but real. An accessory bearing that drones today can seize later, and a seized pulley can throw or shred the belt — which on many cars takes charging, cooling, and steering assist with it. Book it this week.
On cold mornings my car chirps and squeals for the first minute or so, then goes quiet for the rest of the day. Worse when it's damp. What is that?

That's the accessory drive belt (or one of the pulleys it runs on) announcing its age, and the cold-and-damp pattern is the fingerprint. Overnight, the belt cools and stiffens and a film of moisture forms on the pulleys. At startup the belt slips microscopically instead of gripping cleanly, and slip is what squeals. As the engine warms, the belt gets supple, the moisture cooks off, grip returns, and the noise stops — which is why it's gone for the rest of the day.

Two common underlying causes: the belt itself is glazed, cracked, or stretched with age, or the automatic tensioner that keeps it tight has weakened and can't maintain grip. Often both get replaced together, since the labor overlaps.

One firm warning: do not spray belt dressing on it. Dressing quiets the squeal for a few days by making the belt sticky, but it masks the symptom while the wear continues, gums up the pulleys, and makes the eventual diagnosis messier. It's the automotive equivalent of turning up the radio.

Urgency: low today, real over the season. A belt that slips on cold starts is telling you it's near the end of its life; a belt that lets go entirely takes the alternator, water pump, and power steering with it. Mention it at your next service — or sooner if the squeal starts lasting longer or appearing on wet days while driving.
There's a ticking sound from the engine that speeds up as I rev. It's loudest on a cold start and quieter once the engine warms up. Two mechanics' worth of possibilities?

Two main families produce an RPM-locked tick, and the cold-loud/warm-quiet pattern is the classic way to start separating them.

First: an exhaust manifold leak. The manifold bolts to the engine and expands as it heats. A small crack or a failed gasket leaks exhaust in little puffs — one puff per cylinder firing, which is why it ticks in step with revs. Cold, the gap is at its widest and the tick is sharpest; as the metal expands with heat, the gap partly seals and the tick softens. Owners often describe this one as sounding slightly 'spitty' or like a card in bicycle spokes.

Second: valvetrain tick — a hydraulic lifter or lash adjuster that's slow to pump up with oil, or worn valve gear. This tick tends to be more purely mechanical and metallic, and it often (not always) behaves the opposite way or stays constant with temperature. Your first owner move here is free: check the oil level. Low oil, or oil that's overdue and thinned out, starves the lifters at the top of the engine and can cause exactly this tick.

If the oil is full and fresh and the tick persists, it's a shop diagnosis — they listen with a stethoscope to localize it. Neither cause is a stop-driving emergency, but neither is a forever-ignore: a manifold leak can admit fumes near the cabin intake, and a valvetrain tick can be early wear. Note the cold/warm behavior when you book; it's the detail that steers the diagnosis.
My car rattles whenever I go over bumps or rough pavement, but it's silent on smooth roads. Engine speed doesn't matter. Should I worry?

The bump-dependence is the diagnosis's best friend: anything that only speaks when the road hits the car is in the suspension, the exhaust system, or something loose — not the engine, which is why revs are irrelevant.

The most common and most benign culprit is a heat shield: thin metal panels above the exhaust that keep heat off the floor. Their fasteners rust, one corner drops, and the shield buzzes and rattles against the exhaust over every bump. Annoying, cheap to fix, and not dangerous.

The middle tier is exhaust hardware — a broken hanger letting the pipe swing and knock, or a muffler with loose internals. Also inexpensive, mostly.

The tier that deserves prompt attention is suspension: worn sway-bar links are the classic bump-rattle (a clunky rattle over small, sharp bumps at low speed), and worn strut mounts or a loose brake caliper or pad can sound similar. These affect how the car is held together and how it responds in an emergency swerve, so they move the repair from 'sometime' to 'soon.'

Your contribution as the owner: note the conditions precisely. Only over bumps? At what speed? One side or both? Does braking change it (a rattle that stops when you lightly press the brake points at loose pad hardware)? Write that down for the shop — a bump-only rattle can be maddeningly silent on a smooth test drive, and your description may be the only evidence they get.
When I turn the steering wheel all the way to full lock in a parking lot, my car makes a squealing groaning noise. Normal?

Partly — and the 'partly' has a limit you should respect. At full lock, a hydraulic power-steering system is working at maximum pressure: the pump is straining to push the wheels further than they can go. A brief groan or squeal right at the stop is the pump and its belt complaining about that strain, and it happens on many healthy older cars. The correct technique is to back off the wheel a fraction from the stop — never hold a car hard against full lock for more than a second or two, parked or maneuvering. You're just loading the system for no benefit.

Where it stops being normal: if the groan appears well before full lock, if the steering feels notchy or heavy at low speed, or if the noise is new. Then check the one thing an owner may check: the power-steering fluid level, if your car has a reservoir (many newer cars have electric steering and none). The reservoir has marks on it and the manual shows its location. Low fluid makes the pump draw air, and air makes it groan — and low fluid means there's a leak somewhere for a shop to find.

If your car has electric power steering, there's no fluid and no pump; a new groan at full lock would instead be a mechanical noise from the steering or suspension, and that's a 'mention it and have it looked at' item. Either way: ease off the lock, and if the noise is spreading into normal turning, book it.
I just bought a used EV and at low speeds in parking lots it makes a weird musical humming sound. My neighbor says his doesn't. Is something broken?

Almost certainly nothing is broken — what you're hearing is very likely the car's acoustic vehicle alerting system. Electric cars are nearly silent at low speed, which turned out to be a genuine hazard for pedestrians, especially people with vision impairments. Regulations in the US, Europe, and elsewhere therefore require EVs and hybrids to emit a deliberate sound at low speeds (in the US, up to about 19 mph / 30 km/h), and manufacturers compose these sounds — hence the musical, slightly sci-fi hum that starts and stops with low-speed movement.

Why your neighbor's car sounds different: the rule applies to cars built after certain dates, and each maker chose its own sound. An older EV may be silent; a different brand hums a different tune. Volume and character varying by make and year is expected.

How to confirm yours is the designed sound: it should appear only at low speed, be smooth and consistent, and come with no warning lights. What would NOT be normal: grinding, clicking, or a hum that newly appears at highway speed, or any sound accompanied by a warning message. Those get noted and raised at a service visit.

General EV ownership principle, worth adopting early: your diagnostic tools are observation, the owner's manual (which describes the normal sounds), and a service visit for anything new. The high-voltage system itself is never an owner-inspection item.
There's a clunk when I shift from Park to Drive, and another one when I first accelerate from a stop. Rest of the drive is fine. What's clunking?

A clunk at the moment the drivetrain loads up — shifting into gear, or first pressing the accelerator — usually comes from slack somewhere in the chain between the engine and the wheels. When the transmission engages, everything takes up that slack at once, and you hear and feel the take-up as a clunk.

The usual suspects, in rough order of frequency: worn engine or transmission mounts (rubber mounts that hold the powertrain; when the rubber tears, the engine rocks and thumps against its stops), worn universal joints in a rear-wheel-drive shaft, worn CV joints or excessive play in a differential on higher-mileage cars. The mount explanation is especially likely if you can also feel the engine 'shift' with a thud when you get on and off the throttle at low speed.

Your observational contribution: does it clunk once per load change (mounts/lash) or repeatedly with wheel speed (something rotating)? Worse when the car is warm or cold? Those answers narrow it down a lot for the shop.

Urgency: schedule it, don't ignore it. A torn mount left alone lets the engine move more than it should, which strains hoses, wiring, and the other mounts — the classic way one modest repair becomes three. It's not a stop-driving fault as long as it's a single mild clunk, the car drives straight and smooth, and there's no vibration at speed. If it progresses to banging, vibration, or clunks on every gear change, move the appointment up.
After I park, there's a hissing sound from under the hood for a minute or so. Should I be worried?

Usually not — this is one of the normal sounds on the list. When you switch off, the air-conditioning system has high-pressure refrigerant gas on one side and low pressure on the other. With the compressor stopped, the pressures equalize through a small restriction, and that bleed-off hisses quietly for a short while. It's the same sigh you hear from a home air conditioner. No smell, no steam, fades within a minute or two: normal.

The hiss that means something is a coolant leak, and it introduces itself differently. It comes with steam or a visible wisp from one spot, and usually with the sweet, syrupy smell of antifreeze. It may also keep going longer, since it's driven by the cooling system's pressure pushing coolant out through a split hose or a failing cap. The dashboard is your cross-check: has the temperature gauge been creeping up, and is the coolant reservoir level dropping between checks?

So the field test is: hiss alone, briefly, after using the AC on a warm day — file under normal. Hiss plus steam, hiss plus sweet smell, or hiss plus a temperature gauge with ambitions — that's a cooling-system leak, and the car gets looked at before the next long drive. Never investigate a hot cooling system by opening caps; look and smell only.
My car creaks and squeaks going over speed bumps, especially in cold weather. It sounds like an old bed. Is the suspension worn out?

Probably not worn out — that old-bed creak over speed bumps is most often rubber, not metal. Your suspension pivots on rubber bushings and rides on rubber-topped mounts. Rubber stiffens in the cold and dries with age, and a stiff, dry bushing twisting in its bracket as the suspension compresses over a bump creaks exactly like bedsprings. The cold-weather emphasis is the tell: metal wear doesn't much care about temperature, but rubber does.

The supporting evidence for 'benign': the car still rides level, doesn't bounce excessively, tires are wearing evenly, and there are no clunks. Bushing creak is a noise complaint, not a structural one.

What would change the verdict: clunking instead of creaking (loose or worn links and joints), one corner sitting lower than the others, the car continuing to bounce two or three times after a bump (a dead shock absorber — you can test this parked by pushing a corner down hard and watching it settle; it should rise and stop, not oscillate), or uneven tire wear. Those move it to a suspension inspection soon.

Realistically: mention the creak at your next service and have the bushings and shocks looked at then. Shops can confirm bushing condition visually. Replacing creaky bushings purely for silence is a judgment call about money versus annoyance — a legitimate choice either way, as long as the inspection says the parts are tired, not failed.
My car suddenly got a lot louder — a deep rumble from underneath, worst when I accelerate. It happened over a couple of days. What's going on, and is it safe?

A deep rumble that arrived suddenly and swells with acceleration is an exhaust leak or a failed muffler until proven otherwise. The exhaust system is a pipe running the length of the car, and it lives in the worst environment — heat cycles, road salt, vibration. A section rusts through, a joint separates, or the muffler's internals collapse, and suddenly exhaust is escaping before the muffler can quiet it. The sudden onset over days (rather than gradual loudness over years) suggests something let go rather than wore thin.

Drivability: the car will run fine, which tempts people to postpone. Two reasons not to. First, carbon monoxide: exhaust escaping under the car can be drawn into the cabin, especially sitting in traffic or idling with the windows up and the heater drawing air. CO is odorless and its early symptoms — headache, dizziness, drowsiness — are easy to mistake for tiredness. Until it's fixed: don't idle in enclosed spaces, keep fresh air moving through the cabin, and if you ever feel headache-y or woozy while driving, get out into fresh air and take that seriously. Second, in many places a loud or leaking exhaust is an inspection failure and a ticket.

Book it promptly. The repair ranges from a clamp or a short pipe section to a muffler — usually one of the more affordable repairs. Tell the shop where the sound seems to come from (front, middle, rear) and whether it's loudest cold; exhaust leaks often tick or spit when cold and swell as things heat and shift.
Under hard acceleration, especially uphill, my engine makes a rattling 'pinging' sound like marbles in a can. It stops when I ease off. What is that?

That is detonation — engine knock — and the load-and-hill pattern is its signature. Normally the fuel-air mixture burns as a smooth flame front from the spark plug. Under knock, pockets of mixture explode spontaneously from heat and pressure before the flame arrives, and the pressure spikes hammer the piston — that hammering is the marble-rattle you hear. It appears under load (hills, hard acceleration, a heavy car on a hot day) because that's when cylinder pressure and temperature peak, and it stops when you ease off because the pressure drops.

First check, and it's free: what fuel are you using, and what does your manual require? Some engines are designed for premium fuel, and running regular in them invites knock exactly like this. If the manual says premium required, the fix is the fuel. ('Premium recommended' is softer — the engine adapts, with slightly less power.)

If the fuel is correct, the other causes are a shop's list: heavy carbon deposits raising the compression and holding heat, an overheating engine (check your temperature gauge — knock and heat feed each other), or a failed knock sensor that should be telling the computer to retard timing. Persistent knock is not a noise to live with: sustained detonation damages pistons and bearings. Occasional faint ping on a hot hill in a car fed its specified fuel is a 'mention it'; regular knock is a 'book it.'
For about two seconds after I start the engine there's a metallic rattling, then it stops and everything sounds normal. It does it most mornings. Ignore it?

Don't ignore it — a rattle that lives only in the first seconds after startup is telling you a specific story about oil delivery. At rest, oil drains down to the sump. At startup, the pump needs a moment to refill the passages and build pressure. Components that depend on oil pressure to stay tensioned or cushioned — most notably the timing chain tensioner, and in some engines the variable valve timing units — can rattle loosely during that brief dry window until pressure arrives and takes up the slack.

A very short, faint startup rattle on some engine designs is a known characteristic. What moves yours from 'characteristic' to 'symptom' is progression: getting louder, lasting longer (count the seconds — two is different from five), or happening on warm restarts too, not just cold mornings. That progression means the chain is stretching or the tensioner is weakening, and a timing chain that eventually jumps a tooth is an engine-damage event.

Your owner moves: confirm the oil level is at full (a low level lengthens the dry window), and confirm the oil and filter are in date — an oil filter with a failed drain-back valve lets its passages empty overnight and produces exactly this morning rattle, and that's a cheap fix. If level and filter are right and the rattle persists, book a diagnosis and describe it precisely: 'metallic rattle, two seconds, cold starts only.' That sentence saves the shop a day of trying to reproduce it warm.
At low speeds I hear and feel a thump-thump-thump that matches the wheels turning — once per revolution. It fades into the background on the highway. What's the likely cause?

Once-per-revolution is a precise clue: something on one wheel or tire is different at one spot. The shortlist: a nail or screw embedded in the tread (the head strikes the pavement each revolution), a flat spot, or — the one that matters most — a bulge in the tire's sidewall or tread where the internal cords have broken and pressure is ballooning the rubber outward.

Do the owner inspection, parked: turn the steering full lock to expose the front tires, and slowly walk around the car looking at each tire, inside sidewall as best you can with a flashlight, feeling (engine off, car parked) for a lump or bubble in the sidewall. Also look for a screw or nail head in the tread. Run your hand lightly over the tread for a raised or damaged section.

Verdicts: if you find a sidewall bulge, that tire is done — the structure has failed and it can blow out without further warning. Do not take it on the highway; fit the spare if you have one and you're comfortable doing so per the manual, or call roadside service, and drive the short distance to a tire shop at modest speed on the spare. A nail in the tread (not the sidewall) is usually repairable and less urgent, but get it checked within days — it may be leaking slowly, which is also why you check the pressure while you're there. Highway speed masking the thump doesn't mean the problem went away; it means the frequency rose past what you can pick out.
When I turn the key I get one loud CLICK and then nothing. The dash lights are bright and the headlights are strong. Battery?

Probably not the battery — and the bright lights are the evidence. A battery too weak to crank an engine usually can't hold the lights bright either; you'd get dim lights and a machine-gun chattering as the starter solenoid drops in and out. One solid click with strong lights says power is available and is being requested — the starter motor is being told to work and isn't turning.

The click itself is the solenoid (the heavy switch on the starter) slamming shut. What fails after that point: the solenoid's internal contacts burned and pitted with age, so the click happens but full current never reaches the motor; the starter motor itself worn out; or a corroded or loose heavy cable between battery and starter, which can pass enough current for lights but not the hundreds of amps a starter draws.

Owner-level moves are limited to looking: are the battery terminals clean and tight (no white-green crust, no cable you can twist by hand)? Beyond that this is a shop diagnosis — they'll test for voltage arriving at the starter when the key turns, which splits the fault between 'power not arriving' and 'starter not responding' in one measurement.

Don't keep cycling the key twenty times hoping; it rarely helps and can overheat the solenoid. One or two tries, then call it in — and tell the shop 'single click, lights bright.' That sentence rules out half their checklist before they open the hood.
My car makes a rapid clicking sound — like a machine gun — when I try to start it, and the dash lights flicker with each click. What's happening?

That chatter is the classic sound of a battery that's almost — but not quite — able to start the car, and the mechanism is neat. The starter solenoid needs a minimum voltage to stay engaged. Your weak battery delivers just enough: the solenoid pulls in, the starter motor starts to draw its enormous current, the voltage collapses under that load, the solenoid drops out, the load vanishes, the voltage recovers, the solenoid pulls in again... click-click-click, several times a second, with the dash lights flickering in rhythm because they're sharing the collapsing voltage.

So the fault list is short: a discharged battery (lights or a door left ajar overnight, or just an old battery at the end of its life), or corroded/loose terminals strangling the current. The flicker is your clue that this is a supply problem, unlike the single-click case where supply is fine.

What to do: a jump start will very likely get you going — and then the important question becomes 'why was it flat?' If you know you left the lights on, a good drive to recharge and you're done. If nothing explains it, the battery needs a proper test, because a battery that chatters once will usually chatter again within days. Any parts store will load-test it, often free. Also have the terminals cleaned and tightened while you're there — it's cheap and eliminates the other suspect.
Turned the key this morning: total silence, and not a single dashboard light. Completely dead. Where do I even start?

Total electrical silence — no dash lights at all — narrows things usefully, because the dashboard lights need very little power. Even a nearly flat battery usually manages a faint glow. No lights at all suggests the connection between battery and car is interrupted, or the battery is utterly, completely discharged.

Owner-level checks, in order, all visual: First, pop the hood and look at the battery terminals. Is one loose enough to twist by hand? Is there a heavy crust of white or green corrosion insulating the connection? A cable that has worked loose produces exactly this: a car that was fine yesterday and is furniture today. Second, has anything been left on for days — an interior light, a trunk ajar? A small drain over a long weekend can flatten a battery beyond the glow stage. Third, check whether anything at all works — hazard lights, horn, interior light. If the hazards work, power exists and the fault is in the starting circuit; if truly nothing works, it's battery or its main connection.

A jump start is a reasonable next step if you have cables and a donor car, following the manual's connection order. If it starts, don't just celebrate — a battery drained to absolute zero has often been damaged by it, and the cause (loose terminal? parasitic drain? age?) still needs finding. If a jump does nothing, it's a tow and a shop's multimeter. Report the exact symptom — 'no dash lights at all' — because it steers them to the main connection first.
My engine cranks over strongly — rrr-rrr-rrr — but just won't catch and start. The battery sounds healthy. So what's missing?

A strong crank with no start means the starter and battery have done their jobs, and the engine is missing one of the three things it needs to run: fuel, spark, or air (plus correct timing, which rarely fails suddenly). Your diagnostic contribution is to notice this is NOT a battery problem — and to resist the temptation to keep cranking. Long cranking runs the good battery down and can flood the engine with fuel, adding a second problem.

Think about context, because context is what the shop will ask. Did it run fine yesterday? Any recent work done? How much fuel is actually in it — gauges fail, and 'it says a quarter tank' has stranded many people; if in doubt, the cheapest test in all of motoring is adding a gallon of fuel. Any warning lights or a key/security light flashing (an immobilizer that doesn't recognize the key will often let the engine crank but never fire)? Did it sputter and die earlier, or was it perfect until this morning?

Beyond that, this becomes professional diagnosis — fuel pressure, spark, and sensor signals are tested with equipment, and the fuel system in particular is not owner-service territory. Crank in short bursts of a few seconds with pauses if you try again at all, and when you call the shop, lead with: 'cranks strong, won't catch, here's what happened last time it ran.' You've already eliminated the most common cause, and saying so saves everyone time.
On cold mornings my car cranks really slowly — like it's straining — but by afternoon it starts fine. It's getting worse week by week. What should I check?

A slow, labored crank that's worst when cold and worsening over weeks points first at the battery, because cold attacks a battery from both sides: a battery's available power drops sharply as temperature falls, while the engine's demand rises — cold oil is thick, and the starter has to drag the engine through it. A battery with plenty of margin hides this; a battery nearing the end of its life fails the cold test first, in the morning, after sitting all night at its coldest. Afternoon starts, with a warmer battery and an engine that has run recently, are easier.

Check the battery's age before anything else. There's usually a date sticker on top (month/year). Typical service life is 3-5 years, shorter in hot climates. If yours is in or past that window and mornings are getting worse, the pattern is practically a confession — but confirm with a free load test at a parts store rather than buying on suspicion.

The supporting cast: the correct oil viscosity matters (the manual's grade, especially its winter number, e.g. the '5W' in 5W-30, is chosen for cold cranking), and corroded terminals add resistance that hurts most under the starter's huge draw. But the week-by-week worsening trend is the key detail: connections don't usually degrade on a schedule, batteries do. Don't wait for the first morning it doesn't start at all — that morning is coming, and now you know roughly when batteries choose it.
A friend jump-started my car and it ran fine — until I took the jumper cables off, and it died within a minute. Battery's brand new, by the way. What's wrong?

The new battery is innocent, and the test you just ran proves it. Think of it this way: once an engine is running, the alternator is supposed to power the car AND recharge the battery. Your car ran on the donor car's electrical system through the cables. The moment the cables came off, your alternator contributed nothing, the engine drained the new battery's surface charge almost immediately, and it stalled. Diagnosis: the alternator is not charging.

This is the cleanest field test in starting-system diagnosis, and you've already performed it: starts with a jump + dies when the jump is removed = charging system failure. (The mirror-image result — stays running after the cables come off — means the alternator works and the old problem was the battery or a drain.)

Practical notes: don't try to drive it anywhere on battery alone; you'll get minutes, not a trip, and stalling in traffic is the likely ending. It needs a tow, or a mobile mechanic. The shop will confirm with a charging-system test and replace the alternator — and they'll check the belt that drives it first, because a snapped belt produces this exact picture and is a much cheaper fix.

One more thing worth knowing: driving for days with a failing alternator can kill even a new battery by repeatedly deep-discharging it. Once the alternator is replaced, have the battery tested too, so the new part isn't blamed for the old one's damage.
My car jump-started easily and has run perfectly for a week since — starts every morning, no problems. So was it just a fluke? Do I still need to worry?

Mostly good news, and the week of perfect starts is real evidence. Your improvised test separated the suspects: the alternator is charging (or the battery would have gone flat again within a day or two of driving), and the battery can still hold a charge across a week of mornings. What remains is the question of why it was flat that one time.

The innocent explanations are the common ones: a light left on, a door or hatch not fully latched (the car waits, awake, for hours), a phone charger or dashcam sipping power, or a very short-trip pattern in cold weather where each start takes out more than the drive puts back. If you can identify one of those, you've likely found your culprit and the story is over.

The pattern that should bring it back to attention: it happens again with no explanation. A battery that goes flat once for no reason and then behaves is often in the early stage of failing — one weak cell can strand you intermittently before it fails outright. So: get the battery load-tested anyway (free at most parts stores, takes minutes), especially if it's over four years old. A test that says 'healthy' plus a known cause equals peace of mind. A test that says 'marginal' means replace it on your schedule — a planned $200-ish battery at a convenient time beats the same battery as an emergency on the coldest morning of the year.
If my car sits for two or three days, the battery is dead. But if I drive it every day, it's fine. Something is draining it, right? How is that found?

Right — that's the classic parasitic drain pattern, and your observation is the key diagnostic fact: the alternator and battery handle daily use fine, so the charging system works; something keeps drinking power while the car is parked, and two or three days of sipping empties the bucket.

Every modern car has a small legitimate draw when off — clocks, keyless-entry receivers, security systems, computers' memories — typically a few tens of milliamps, which a healthy battery tolerates for weeks. A parasitic drain is a draw well above that: a glovebox or trunk light whose switch failed, a module that never goes to sleep because a door switch lies to it, an aftermarket accessory wired to constant power, a stuck relay keeping a fan or pump circuit alive.

How a shop finds it: they connect a meter in series with the battery, wait for the car's systems to fully sleep (which can take 20-45 minutes on modern cars — test too early and everything looks guilty), measure the draw, and then pull fuses one at a time until the draw collapses. The fuse that kills it names the circuit, and the hunt narrows to components on that circuit.

Your contribution, beyond the 'two to three days' timeline (state it exactly — it's how they verify the fix): mention anything aftermarket or recently installed, and any odd behavior — a light you've seen on, a fan running after shutdown, a door that needs slamming. After the repair, the honest verification is the same test that found it: let it sit three days and see if it starts.
The parts store guy says my battery is from 2019 and I should just replace it. The car starts fine most days. Is he upselling me, or is seven years really borrowed time?

He's not upselling you — seven years is genuinely borrowed time. The typical car battery lasts 3-5 years; in hot climates, often less, because heat is what ages the plates inside. A battery that has reached seven years has outlived most of its siblings, and batteries rarely send a polite warning letter before failing: the most common pattern is 'fine, fine, fine, dead' — often on the first cold morning of the year, because cold slashes the power a worn battery can deliver while the engine demands more.

But 'old' isn't the same as 'proven bad,' and you don't have to buy on age alone. Ask for the load test — most parts stores do it free in the parking lot. The tester draws a heavy load and measures how the battery holds voltage, then reports its remaining capacity against its rating. A seven-year-old battery that still tests at, say, 80% of its rating can serve on; one testing at half its rating is a countdown.

The arithmetic of the decision: a planned replacement costs the battery's price at a time of your choosing. An unplanned one costs the battery plus a tow or a missed morning, usually in bad weather. Given the age, even a passing test buys limited confidence — if the budget allows, replacing a seven-year-old battery before winter is one of the highest-value preventive spends in car ownership. If you keep it, at least keep jumper cables or a booster pack in the trunk and know the battery has told you its age.
My push-button start says 'Key Not Detected' even though the key fob is right there in my pocket. Is the car broken?

Almost certainly the car is fine — the fob's battery is dead or nearly. The fob contains a small coin battery (often a CR2032) that powers its radio transmissions, and they typically last 2-4 years. When it fades, the car can no longer hear the fob's signal from your pocket, so it reports, accurately from its point of view, that no key is present.

The rescue procedure is built into nearly every push-button car and it's in your manual: hold the fob itself directly against the start button (or place it in the designated slot or spot the manual shows) and press the button with it. The button has a short-range reader that can power and interrogate a dead fob at contact distance — the same technology as a tap-to-pay card. That gets you started and driving.

Then replace the fob battery: it's an owner task on most fobs — a seam you can pry with a coin or small screwdriver, the battery size printed on the old one — and costs a few dollars. If you have a second fob, notice it probably needs one too, since they age together.

If a fresh fob battery doesn't cure it, or the message appears with both fobs, then it becomes a car-side receiver issue for a shop. But nine times out of ten, this is a $5 coin cell wearing a very alarming costume.
My car starts and then stalls after about a second, every time. Starts fine, dies immediately. Any ideas?

Starts-then-dies-in-a-second is a distinctive pattern with two leading suspects, and a dashboard light helps separate them.

Suspect one: the immobilizer. Modern keys contain a transponder the car must recognize. If it doesn't — a damaged key, a key whose chip failed, sometimes a key that was recently replaced or a heavy keyring interfering — many cars are programmed to allow a start and then cut the engine a second later, or crank without firing. The clue is a flashing key-shaped or padlock light on the dash while this happens. Try your spare key: if the spare starts and runs, you've diagnosed it from the driver's seat, and the fix is a key, not an engine.

Suspect two: the engine gets its starting fuel but can't sustain running — a failing fuel pump that primes but can't keep pressure, or an airflow sensor fault that makes the computer's fuel calculations collapse once the start-up enrichment ends. These come with no security light, and diagnosis needs a fuel-pressure gauge and a scanner.

What not to do: don't keep cycling it twenty times, and don't hold the throttle open to 'catch' it — on a modern drive-by-wire car that rarely helps and can confuse the idle learning. Try the spare key once. If the security light is flashing, it's a key/immobilizer issue for a dealer or a locksmith with the right equipment. If not, it's a tow-and-diagnose item — and 'starts, runs one second, dies, every time' is exactly the description to give them; that consistency is information.

Once in a while my car won't start — usually after a short stop, like getting gas. If I wait 15-20 minutes, it starts like nothing happened. The shop couldn't find anything because it always works there. Help?

You have the most frustrating fault in motoring — an intermittent no-start — and the fact that the shop can't reproduce it is expected, not a brush-off. But your description contains the diagnostic gold, so let's organize it.

The pattern 'fails hot, after a short stop, recovers after a cool-down wait' points strongly at heat-related failures. The leading suspect is the starter motor itself: a worn starter can fail when heat-soaked (a hot engine bay after a short stop is actually the hottest a starter gets, because airflow stops while engine heat soaks into it), then work again when it cools. Corroded or loose cable connections behave similarly — heat expands metal and a marginal connection opens up. On some cars, a failing crankshaft position sensor quits when hot and revives when cool, though that usually causes a crank-but-no-start rather than silence.

Critical detail to pin down for next time: when it fails, WHAT does it do — single click, chatter, silence, or crank-no-start? And do the dash lights behave normally? Note the outside temperature, how long you'd driven, how long you waited. A phone video of a failed attempt is worth a page of description.

Strategy with the shop: describe the pattern and ask them to test under the failing conditions — a good shop will heat-soak the car and try repeatedly, and test the starter's draw and the connections while hot. Intermittents are found by reproducing conditions, not by scanning a healthy car. Keep notes; the pattern is the diagnosis's raw material.
When I try to start my car there's a horrible screeching/grinding noise and the engine doesn't turn over properly. I stopped trying. Right call?

Right call — every attempt grinds away more of the parts involved. That screech is metal gear teeth failing to mesh. The starter motor has a small gear that slides out to engage a large ring gear on the engine's flywheel or flexplate, spins the engine, then retracts. When the starter's gear is worn, or its mechanism can't push it fully into mesh, you get spinning teeth gnashing against the ring gear instead of engaging it — the screech you heard.

Why stopping matters: the ring gear is part of the engine's rotating assembly. Replacing a starter is a modest job; replacing a ring gear whose teeth have been chewed up means separating the engine and transmission — many hours of labor. The screech is the sound of a small repair auditioning to become a large one, and each crank attempt helps it audition.

Occasionally the cause is more benign — a starter that's loose on its mount can sit misaligned — but that's still a shop's eyes and hands, not a 'keep trying' situation. The car gets towed, and your report is simple: 'screeching on crank, engine doesn't turn, I stopped after the first try.' Mechanics will quietly appreciate that last clause; it often means the ring gear survived. If you absolutely must move the car, it moves on a tow truck, not under its own power.
My EV won't go into READY mode. The screens light up but it won't drive. A friend says 'it's probably just the 12-volt battery, like a normal car.' Is he right?

He's right more often than you'd expect. An EV has two electrical systems: the high-voltage traction battery that drives the motors, and an ordinary 12-volt battery — the same kind as in a gasoline car — that runs the computers, displays, lights, and, crucially, the contactors that connect the big battery. When you press the start button, the 12-volt system boots the computers and closes those contactors. If the 12-volt battery is weak or dead, the screens may glow dimly or behave erratically, but the car cannot bring its high-voltage system online, so READY never lights and the car won't move.

This catches EV owners out because the traction battery can be at 80% charge and the car is still stranded by a small lead-acid battery that's three or four years old. EVs are actually hard on their 12-volt batteries in a subtle way: they're charged from the traction pack by a DC-DC converter, sometimes only at intervals, and short-trip patterns can leave them undercharged.

What you may do: follow your manual. Many EVs permit jump-starting the 12-volt battery from another car, using specified jump posts — the manual gives the exact procedure and connection points, and you follow it to the letter or not at all. Replacing the 12-volt battery is also often an owner-possible job per the manual. What you never touch: anything with orange cabling — that's the high-voltage system, and it is not owner territory under any circumstances.

If a jump per the manual brings READY back, drive to have the 12-volt battery tested and replaced if it fails; if it doesn't, it's a tow and a dealer-level diagnosis.
My car takes a long time cranking after it sits overnight, and I've started noticing a gasoline smell around it in the morning. Once it starts, it's fine all day. What's going on?

Take the smell seriously first, because it changes the category of this problem. A gasoline odor around a parked car means fuel vapor is escaping somewhere it shouldn't — a seeping line, a failing seal, an injector leaking down overnight. Fuel systems are sealed and pressurized precisely because gasoline vapor is flammable, so this is not a 'monitor it' symptom: park the car outside rather than in an attached garage until it's looked at, keep it away from ignition sources (no smoking nearby, obviously, but also water heaters and the like), and get it to a shop promptly — towed if the smell is strong or you can see any wetness or dripping.

The long crank and the smell are likely the same fault telling one story. The fuel system is supposed to hold pressure while the car sits. If a leak lets pressure bleed off overnight — or an injector drips fuel into a cylinder — then in the morning the pump needs several seconds of cranking to rebuild pressure before the engine can fire. Once running, the pump maintains pressure easily and the car behaves all day. By evening it starts the slow bleed again.

Diagnosis and repair are professional work: the fuel system is pressurized, flammable, and not owner-serviceable, and your role ends at observation. But your observation is valuable — report both halves: 'long crank after sitting overnight, fuel smell around the car in the morning, fine once started.' That combination points the technician straight at a pressure-loss test instead of a general tune-up.
There's a fresh puddle under my car every morning. How do I figure out what fluid it is before I panic?

Fluid identification is a process of elimination by color, feel, smell, and position — and most owners can narrow it down in two minutes with a piece of white cardboard.

Slide the cardboard under the drip area overnight; in the morning you'll have a clean sample. Now read it. Clear and watery, no smell: water — almost always air-conditioning condensation, the one innocent puddle. Bright green, pink, or orange, thin, with a sweet smell: coolant. Dark brown to black, slippery, earthy smell: engine oil. Red or pinkish-red, slippery: transmission fluid or power-steering fluid. Pale yellow-brown, very slippery, with a distinctive acrid smell: brake fluid — that one is not a wait-and-see; see below. Blue and watery near the front: windshield washer fluid, harmless.

Position tells the rest: front of the car points at the engine and its systems; middle, the transmission; near a wheel, brake or wheel-bearing grease. Smear a drop between your fingers — oil and transmission fluid feel slick; coolant feels slightly slippery-sweet; water feels like water.

The action ladder: water — ignore. Washer fluid — ignore, refill. Oil or coolant — check the relevant level (dipstick, reservoir), note the rate, book a shop visit. Transmission — book it soon. Brake fluid, or ANY fluid plus a soft brake pedal — do not drive; tow. And photograph the cardboard: 'red, middle of the car, about a teaspoon a night' is a better opening line for a mechanic than 'it's leaking something.'
Every day after I drive with the AC on, there's a puddle of water under the passenger side of my car. My neighbor says his car does it too. Normal?

Completely normal — this is the one puddle that needs no action at all. Your air conditioner works by pulling heat and moisture out of the cabin air. The moisture condenses on the cold evaporator, exactly like dew on a cold glass, and the car routes that water through a drain tube that exits underneath, typically around the front passenger footwell area. On a humid day after a drive with the AC running, a puddle the size of a dinner plate is unremarkable.

The checks that confirm it's this and nothing else: the liquid is clear, has no smell, isn't slippery, and evaporates like water. It appears only after AC use. It never appears on a dry morning after the car sat unused all weekend. All fluids that matter — coolant, oil, transmission, brake — are colored, slippery, or smelly; plain water is none of those.

The one variant worth attention is the reverse problem: if you ever find the front passenger carpet wet and musty, the same drain tube may be clogged and the condensation is backing up into the cabin instead of dripping outside. That's a minor shop fix (they clear the drain), not a crisis, but left alone it grows mildew.

So: water under the car on a humid afternoon — the car is sweating, as designed. Save your worry for puddles with color, slickness, or smell.
My coolant reservoir keeps dropping. I can smell something sweet near the front of the car, and there's a crusty greenish deposit around one of the hoses. Can I just keep topping it up?

Topping up is a legitimate short-term measure — with rules — but understand that you're managing a leak, not fixing one, and the crusty deposit has already told you where it is. That greenish-white crust is dried coolant minerals left behind as leaking coolant evaporates at a hose connection; the sweet smell is ethylene glycol vapor. The system is losing coolant slowly, probably at that hose clamp or a hose that's hardening with age.

The rules for topping up: only check and fill when the engine is completely cold — never open the reservoir or radiator cap on a hot engine, because the system is pressurized and can erupt scalding coolant. Fill to the MAX line with the coolant type your manual specifies (coolant types are not all compatible; color alone is not a reliable guide), or with distilled water only as a short stopgap in a warm climate.

Why 'just keep topping up' has an expiry date: the leak will not heal, and leaks tend to fail suddenly rather than gradually — a hose that's seeping at the clamp today can split next month, and then the coolant loss is measured in minutes and the engine overheats. Also track your rate: 'a cup a week' versus 'the reservoir every two days' are different urgencies. Write it down.

Book the shop visit and tell them about the crust — you've localized the leak for them, which is half the diagnostic labor. The repair is usually a hose and clamps: cheap. The engine it protects is not.
There are oil spots on my driveway. A few drops each night. The car runs fine. How do I tell if it's a 'keep an eye on it' seep or a real leak?

Measure it — the difference between a seep and a leak is a rate, and rates can be measured with the dipstick and a calendar instead of guessed from driveway stains (which exaggerate: a teaspoon of oil spreads into an alarming-looking spot on concrete).

Start with the dipstick at the full mark, note the odometer, and check weekly under consistent conditions — engine warm, parked level, a few minutes after shutdown. The marks on most dipsticks span about one quart (roughly a liter) from low to full. So the arithmetic is simple: if you lose the distance from full to the low mark over 3,000 miles, that's a quart per 3,000 miles — a seep, typical of aging gaskets, and a 'monitor and mention at service' issue. If you're adding a quart every 500 miles, that's a real leak demanding a repair appointment.

Meanwhile, the cardboard test localizes it: clean cardboard under the engine overnight, then note where the drips land relative to the engine — front, rear, one side — and take a photo. Drips at the very back of the engine can be a rear main seal (labor-heavy); drips at the front or around the edges of covers are often valve-cover or oil-pan gaskets (more modest).

Two escalation triggers regardless of rate: oil dripping onto a hot exhaust component (you'd smell burning oil after drives — that's a fire-risk and smoke issue, book promptly), and any sudden increase in rate. And keep the level between the marks while you monitor; running low is how a cheap gasket turns into an expensive engine.
Found reddish fluid leaking under the middle-front of my car. What is it, and can I check anything myself?

Red narrows it to two systems: automatic transmission fluid (which starts life red and translucent) and, on many cars, power-steering fluid (often the same fluid). Position helps: middle-front fits both the transmission and the steering rack, which sits low across the front of the car.

Your owner checks: if your car has a power-steering reservoir (the manual shows it; many newer cars have electric steering and none), check its level against the marks — a low reservoir plus a groaning noise when you turn the wheel would convict the steering system. Transmission fluid level, by contrast, is not owner-checkable on most modern cars — the dipstick has been deleted on many models and the check is a shop procedure done at a specific fluid temperature.

How urgent: a few drops of transmission fluid is a 'book it this week' item, not a tow — but don't shelve it. Transmissions tolerate low fluid badly; slipping and harsh shifts are the symptoms of a starving transmission, and by the time it slips, wear has begun. If the puddle is large, the car is leaving a trail, or shifting has already changed, park it and call.

One identification caution: old transmission fluid darkens toward brown and can be mistaken for engine oil. The cardboard test helps — fresh drops of transmission fluid usually keep a reddish tint at the edge of the stain, and it's typically thinner and less sooty than used engine oil.
